reference_title: Wood Handbook: Wood as an Engineering Material (USDA Forest Products Laboratory, General Technical Report FPL-GTR-282, 2021)

sections.title: Nails
sections.summary: Covers nail types (Fig 8-1), withdrawal resistance from side grain (Eq 8-1 smooth-shank, Eq 8-2a/b annularly threaded), and lateral resistance -- both the pre-1991 empirical proportional-limit equation (Eq 8-2, p=K*D^1.5, Table 8-4) and the post-1991 5% offset yield-limit model (Table 8-5).
sections.body: Nails are classified by shank form (smooth, annularly threaded, helically threaded, barbed) and surface treatment (bright, cement-coated, zinc-coated), each affecting withdrawal resistance (Fig 8-1). Withdrawal resistance of common (smooth-shank) nails driven into side grain of seasoned wood follows Eq 8-1 (p=54.12*G^2.5*D*L, metric); annularly threaded nails follow the higher-holding Eq 8-2a (p=77.57*G^2*D*L). Lateral resistance historically used a pre-1991 proportional-limit empirical equation (also numbered '8-2' in this printed edition -- a citation collision documented in this module's fastenings.py -- p=K*D^1.5, K from Table 8-4) defined at 0.38 mm joint slip; current design uses the 5% offset yield-limit (European Yield Model) theory (Table 8-5), computing dowel bearing strength from specific gravity (Eq 8-3) and checking four governing yield modes (Is, IIIm, IIIs, IV).
key_points: Nail withdrawal: Eq 8-1 (smooth shank), Eq 8-2a/b (annularly threaded)
Nail lateral resistance: pre-1991 empirical p=K*D^1.5 (also labeled Eq 8-2, Table 8-4) vs. post-1991 yield-limit model (Table 8-5)
Dowel bearing strength Fe is estimated from specific gravity via Eq 8-3, feeding the yield-limit model for ALL dowel-type fasteners (nails, screws, bolts, lag screws)
sections.applicability: Sizing and checking nailed connections for withdrawal and lateral (shear) loading.

sections.title: Spikes, Staples, and Drift Bolts
sections.summary: Spikes and staples follow similar principles to nails (larger-diameter withdrawal/lateral relations for spikes; specialized wire-staple behavior). Drift bolts/pins use a printed withdrawal equation (Eq 8-9) analogous in form to the nail/screw withdrawal equations.
sections.body: Spikes are larger-diameter nails, generally following the same withdrawal/lateral mechanics as nails with spike-specific coefficients (not separately digitized in this module -- use the nail equations with the spike's actual diameter where the handbook's spike-specific guidance permits). Staples are used extensively in sheathing/panel attachment with their own withdrawal/lateral test-based values (chart-based, not printed as closed-form equations). Drift bolts or pins (long, unthreaded rods driven into prebored holes 3.2 mm smaller than the bolt) resist withdrawal per Eq 8-9 (p=45.51*G^2*D*L), assuming average behavior across species.
key_points: Spikes follow nail-type mechanics at larger diameters
Staples are chart/table-based in this handbook, not closed-form equations
Drift bolt withdrawal: Eq 8-9 (average relationship across species)
sections.applicability: Heavy-timber connections (drift bolts/pins) and sheathing attachment (spikes, staples).

sections.title: Wood Screws
sections.summary: Wood screw types (Fig 8-7), withdrawal resistance (Eq 8-10), and the pre-1991 empirical lateral resistance equation (Eq 8-13, p=K*D^2, Table 8-4); Table 8-9 gives shank diameter by screw gauge. Post-1991 lateral resistance uses the same yield-limit model as nails (Table 8-5, screw-specific mode formulas).
sections.body: Wood screws (flathead, roundhead, ovalhead, Fig 8-7) resist withdrawal from side grain per Eq 8-10 (p=108.25*G^2*D*L), applicable for properly sized lead holes (~70% of root diameter in softwoods, ~90% in hardwoods). Pre-1991 lateral (proportional-limit) resistance follows Eq 8-13 (p=K*D^2, Table 8-4), requiring penetration of the threaded part >= 7x the shank diameter. Post-1991 design uses the yield-limit model (Table 8-5), with the screw-specific IIIs and IV mode formulas differing slightly from the nail forms (a 1.75 vs 2.0 coefficient in mode IV, reflecting the more consistent, threaded engagement of a screw vs. a smooth nail shank).
key_points: Screw withdrawal: Eq 8-10; screw shank diameter by gauge in Table 8-9
Pre-1991 lateral resistance: Eq 8-13 (p=K*D^2, Table 8-4)
Post-1991 yield-limit model uses screw-specific mode IIIs/IV coefficients (Table 8-5)
sections.applicability: Sizing and checking screwed connections for withdrawal and lateral (shear) loading.

sections.title: Lag Screws
sections.summary: Lag screw withdrawal (Eq 8-14) and pre-1991 lateral resistance (Eq 8-15, p=K*D^2) with multiplication factors for side-member thickness (Table 8-10) and perpendicular-to-grain loading (Table 8-11).
sections.body: Lag screws (large, coarse-threaded wood screws typically installed with a wrench) resist direct withdrawal per Eq 8-14 (p=125.4*G^1.5*D^0.75*L), developed independently of the wood-screw equation but giving similar results. Pre-1991 lateral resistance parallel to grain follows Eq 8-15 (p=K*D^2, Table 8-4), with a base assumption of side-member thickness 3.5x the shank diameter and main-member penetration 7-11x the diameter; Table 8-10 gives multiplication factors for other side-member-thickness ratios and Table 8-11 for loading perpendicular to grain. Lead-hole quality (Fig 8-8) strongly affects achieved capacity.
key_points: Lag screw withdrawal: Eq 8-14
Lag screw lateral resistance (pre-1991): Eq 8-15 (p=K*D^2), with Table 8-10 (thickness factor) and Table 8-11 (perpendicular-to-grain factor)
Post-1991 design uses the same yield-limit model as nails/screws (Table 8-5)
sections.applicability: Heavy connections (ledger attachment, hardware-to-timber connections) using lag screws.

sections.title: Bolts
sections.summary: Bolted-connection behavior: bearing stress of wood under bolts (both parallel and perpendicular to grain, historically via test curves Figs 8-9 to 8-13), loads at an angle to grain (via the general Hankinson formula, Eq 8-16), steel side plates, bolt quality, member thickness effects, multi-member joints, spacing/edge/end distance, and bolt-hole quality. Both the historical (pre-1991 allowable stress) and current (post-1991 yield model) design bases are described.
sections.body: Bolted-connection capacity historically was characterized by proportional-limit bearing-stress test curves as functions of L/D ratio (length-to-diameter, Figs 8-9 to 8-12) and side-member thickness (Fig 8-13), separately for parallel- and perpendicular-to-grain loading; bearing at an intermediate angle to grain uses the general Hankinson formula (Eq 8-16), which appears throughout the handbook wherever a parallel/perpendicular-to-grain property must be combined at an angle. Bolt-hole surface quality from drilling rate/speed (Fig 8-14) measurably affects joint load-deformation behavior (Fig 8-15). Modern (post-1991) bolted-joint design uses the same yield-limit model (Table 8-5) as nails/screws, with the bolt's actual diameter and bending yield stress (ASTM F1575).
key_points: Bearing stress at an angle to grain (bolts, lag screws) uses the general Hankinson formula, Eq 8-16
Historical bolt design used proportional-limit test curves (Figs 8-9 to 8-13, graphical, not digitized)
Current bolt design uses the same yield-limit model (Table 8-5) as nails/screws
sections.applicability: Bolted timber connection design, and any wood bearing/loading problem at an angle to the grain.

sections.title: Connector Joints (Split Rings and Shear Plates)
sections.summary: Split-ring and shear-plate timber connectors (Figs 8-16/8-17) develop much higher joint capacity than bolts alone by engaging a larger bearing area; capacity relates to specific gravity (Figs 8-18 to 8-23, test-curve based) with net-section, spacing/end-distance, and multiple-fastener-joint modification rules.
sections.body: Split-ring connectors (precut grooves plus a metal ring and through-bolt, Fig 8-16) and shear-plate connectors (flush-mounted, used with wood or steel side plates, Fig 8-17) develop substantially higher parallel- and perpendicular-to-grain load capacity than an unassisted bolt, by engaging a larger, more uniform bearing area. Design capacity is empirically related to wood specific gravity (Figs 8-18 through 8-23, test-curve-based -- not printed as closed-form equations), then modified for net section at the connector, end distance and spacing (Fig 8-25), cross bolts, and multiple-fastener-joint group effects. Member thickness below an optimum value reduces achievable capacity (Fig 8-24).
key_points: Split rings and shear plates substantially outperform plain bolts by engaging more bearing area
Capacity vs. specific gravity relationships are printed as test curves (Figs 8-18 to 8-23), not closed-form equations
Net section, end distance/spacing, and member thickness all modify achievable capacity
sections.applicability: High-capacity timber connections (glulam trusses, heavy timber construction) using split-ring/shear-plate connectors; graphical design data not digitized as closed-form equations in this module.

sections.title: Metal Plate Connectors and Joist Hangers
sections.summary: Metal plate connectors (toothed plates pressed into wood faces, typically for trusses, Fig 8-26) and joist hangers (formed steel brackets, Fig 8-28) are proprietary/tested hardware systems; design values come from manufacturer testing per ASTM/ICC-ES standards rather than the handbook's own closed-form equations.
sections.body: Metal plate connectors (Fig 8-26), used almost exclusively in factory-fabricated wood trusses, develop capacity through many small teeth pressed into the wood faces on each side of a joint; typical load-slip behavior is shown in Fig 8-27, but design values are established by full-scale ASTM testing programs rather than closed-form mechanics equations. Joist hangers (Fig 8-28) are formed sheet-steel brackets whose capacity is governed by the lowest of several failure modes (hanger steel, fasteners, wood bearing) and, similarly, is established by testing rather than closed-form equations in this handbook.
key_points: Metal plate connectors and joist hangers are proprietary, tested hardware -- capacity is NOT given by closed-form handbook equations
Design values for both come from standardized full-scale testing (ASTM/ICC-ES), out of scope for this module
sections.applicability: Truss and joist-hanger connections; proprietary/tested hardware, not digitized as equations.

sections.title: Fastener Head Embedment
sections.summary: Embedment of a fastener head (e.g., nail or screw head pulling through sheathing) is characterized empirically by maximum embedment load vs. fastener perimeter (Fig 8-29) and load at a specified embedment vs. bearing area (Fig 8-30), by species.
sections.body: Head pull-through (embedment) resistance -- relevant to sheathing/panel attachment where the fastener head, not the shank, may govern capacity -- is characterized by test relationships between maximum embedment load and fastener perimeter (Fig 8-29), and between load at 1.27 mm embedment and fastener bearing area (Fig 8-30), for several wood species. Graphical/test-curve based; not printed as closed-form equations.
key_points: Head embedment (pull-through) can govern capacity in sheathing/panel connections
Characterized by test curves (Figs 8-29/8-30) vs. fastener perimeter/bearing area, not closed-form equations
sections.applicability: Checking fastener head pull-through in panel/sheathing attachment; graphical data, not digitized as equations.
